subjects.displayTitle: Steadfastness, perseverance and faithfulness: firmly settled as the immovable mountain
subjects.introduction: What does it mean to be steadfast, and what holds a soul firm when everything around it shakes? These 300 chosen quotations include every verified authorized selection in the compilation. They open with the station of steadfastness, which Bahá’u’lláh calls the first word of the Crimson Book and the crown of all deeds, and then ask what steadfastness is and how it is attained. The images of the immovable mountain and the firmly rooted tree lead into the winds of tests that show who is firm, and into patience, the inward side of endurance. Later sections treat steadfastness in love, firmness in the Covenant, faithfulness, perseverance in effort and service, and trust in God. The guide then turns to the steadfastness of Bahá’u’lláh and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá and to the martyrs and believers who stood firm, and ends with prayers to be made steadfast and numbered with those whom nothing could deter. Most passages are Tablets and prayers of Bahá’u’lláh and Tablets and reported talks of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá, joined by writings of the Báb; seven supplied extracts, among them letters written on behalf of Shoghi Effendi and a verse from the Laws of Manu, follow at the end with their catalogue status.

This section asks what steadfastness is and how it is gained. Bahá’u’lláh defines it as knowing God alone as the One who prevails over all things and seeing all else as evanescent, and as being independent of all save God. The beginning of the matter is the recognition of God and its end is steadfastness in His Cause; once that station is reached, steadfastness is one of two things obligatory on every soul. True listening, He writes, is to hear the call of the All-Merciful and then remain so steadfast that the denial of all peoples could not deflect one from the straight path, and a prayer adds that none can stand firm save one detached from all else. He bids the friends reflect upon its degrees and seek it with lowliness. The Báb bids the believer be steadfast as though standing in the presence of God. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá names silence and quietude among its causes, deeds and self-sacrifice as its evidence, the qualities of the holy as its proof and contentment as its companion, and in a reported talk explains how to stand firm in a torrent.

Here the readings turn to the images by which the Writings picture firmness. In the Kitáb-i-Aqdas Bahá’u’lláh bids the believers be as firmly settled as the immovable mountain, and says that whoever has recognized the Source of His utterance will welcome the shafts of the enemy. He calls the people of God to be as mountains that the blasts of allusions cannot move, inwardly surging oceans and outwardly firm as mountains, and so steadfast that even should all the Manifestations of His Names descend to turn them, they would not turn. The Báb writes that one who is like a mountain no storm can move has attained the summit of the Cause. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá asks the friends to be mountains of iron and impregnable walls, blessed trees planted in the soil of the Covenant, and so constant that a single surviving believer would withstand all the peoples of the earth. Reported talks warn against being straw in the wind or a chameleon that changes colour, and give a commandment, as a covenant, to be steadfast as a rock that no storm can move.

This section takes up the tests that make steadfastness visible. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá explains that it is God’s way to test the sincere with great trials, that until fierce winds blow the firm tree cannot be told from the unstable one, and that firmness in comfort and safety is something even a weak ant can manage, while skill shows when the captain steers through the storm. Gold melted in the fire, a diamond under the millstone, a candle shining while an owl hides in a dark corner: such are his images for those who stand. Bahá’u’lláh observes how many strong souls wavered when the winds of tests blew and how many weak ones were made steadfast, how leaves fell from the tree of His Cause while others clung to it, and how strange it is that those who claim steadfastness are shaken by the merest whiff of vain imaginings. Reported talks add that without trials nothing is accomplished and that a different spirituality appears in one who remains firm. The Báb bids the believer let nothing destined in this Cause disturb him.

Bahá’u’lláh observes how many strong souls wavered when the winds of tests blew and how many weak ones were made steadfast, how leaves fell from the tree of His Cause while others clung to it, and how strange it is that those who claim steadfastness are shaken by the merest whiff of vain imaginings. Reported talks add that without trials nothing is accomplished and that a different spirituality appears in one who remains firm. The Báb bids the believer let nothing destined in this Cause disturb him.

Patience is the inward side of steadfastness, and this section gathers counsels on it. In the Súriy-i-Haykal Bahá’u’lláh recalls that He withstood His trials with forbearance and enjoined patience and fortitude on God’s servants. He bids the believer be patient even as his Lord was patient, and then yet more patient, for the end is for such as endure with constancy; this, He says, is the day of patience, and the loved ones should cling to the hem of patience through His Name, the All-Patient. The Báb calls for beautiful patience and recalls the promise that those patient under the words of enemies receive the reward of a thousand martyrs. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá describes believers whose patience did not fail though their hearts burned, who were steadfast upon burning coals, and who in affliction comforted others, their faces glowing with radiant acquiescence. He calls the shirt of patience the most adorning garment, quotes the saying that the patient are rewarded while God’s decree is done either way, and tells how his own trials passed away through patience and calm.

Steadfastness in the Writings is first of all steadfastness in love. In the Hidden Words the sign of love is fortitude under God’s decree and patience under His trials, and in the Lawh-i-Ahmad Bahá’u’lláh asks that the believer be so steadfast in His love that the heart shall not waver though the swords of the enemies rain blows; the same Tablet bids him rely upon God. He names steadfastness in His love as the first of what is required, a steadfastness that takes no account of enemy or pretender, and says it endures even should one find oneself alone in love for one’s Lord. Prayers and passages in His own voice add that in God’s love every fire is light and every sorrow gladness, that none of the kings of the earth can hinder Him from extolling God, and that His soul would not be emptied of love were He slain; in the Fire Tablet He has risen up in faithfulness at the place of sacrifice. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá asks the friends to accept every tribulation in their love for God, and his verses vow not to turn away whatever fire, blood or prison may come.

In reported talks he says that nothing is harder than following the straight path, since many take ten steps and stop, and likens the worker in the Cause to a gardener and to a traveller who keeps walking. Bahá’u’lláh bids the believer go straight on and persevere in what the Pen of God commands, persevere in service and preserve the station conferred upon him, and make good what has been lost, for time is more precious than red sulphur. The Báb promises a holy station to those who strive.

Steadfastness rests on trust, and this section gathers counsels on reliance upon God. In the Súriy-i-Mulúk Bahá’u’lláh bids the believer place his whole trust in his Lord in all circumstances and not rely on his treasures, and in the Words of Wisdom He names trust in God, submission to His command and contentment with His pleasure as the source of all good. He writes that it is incumbent on every man to trust in God’s bounties and arise to teach His Cause, that one must lift the gaze from outward causes, and that if outward means fail one should not be disheartened, since every matter has its appointed time. A leaf, He says, moves only with the divine breeze, so an opposer might better try to stop the winds; fear and anxiety do not befit the people of truth. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá bids the friends rely upon God, Who turns trouble into ease, never lose hope, since man is immersed in a sea of His blessings, and never let outward circumstances worry them. In a reported talk he says that he has been under God’s protection from the day he was born.

Before the believers come the passages in which Bahá’u’lláh and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá speak of Their own steadfastness. In the Lawh-i-Rasúl Bahá’u’lláh writes that He stood against His enemies manifest as the sun, never for an instant seeking to preserve His own life, His fortress His reliance on God. Elsewhere He says that He never hesitated in advancing the Cause nor compromised with anyone, that tribulations shall not prevent Him from mentioning the Lord of Names, and that the winds of tribulation cannot extinguish this Lamp. Were the idolaters to put Him to death at every moment, they would find Him patient and thankful; the Youth, if drowned, would praise God among the fish of the sea, and on the cross would make mention of His God. He speaks of Husayn, whose intimacy with tribulations is as the intimacy of the lover with the beloved, and of the Wronged One who has clung to gracious patience, for whom in God’s path fire is light. In a reported talk ‘Abdu’l-Bahá recalls praising God each morning of His forty years in prison for another day of service.

This section gathers accounts of believers who stood firm in life and in death. In the Lawh-i-Ra’ís Bahá’u’lláh says of His companions that their blood implores to be spilt in His path, and in another Tablet He tells of a mother who urged her son to offer himself in the path of God and not betray his faith; His recorded recollections of imprisonment tell of fellow-prisoners who bore hunger without a murmur. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá, in the Memorials of the Faithful and in Tablets, writes of an enraptured lover of God who never gave way, of the martyrs of Yazd and Isfahan whose steadfastness is the greatest proof of the friends’ sincerity, of prisoners from whom no moan was heard, of the loved ones of Nayriz, of the steadfast believers of London, and of women who outstripped men in the arena of firmness. Reported talks tell of the besieged in the fortress who ate the leather of their shoes, of the martyrs of Yazd who did not defend themselves, and of Persian believers who cried ‘Yá Bahá’u’l-Abhá!’ under the sword, and they contrast Peter’s denial with the constancy of the followers of Bahá’u’lláh.

The closing prayers ask to be numbered with those whom nothing could turn aside. Bahá’u’lláh’s prayers ask God to number the one praying with those whom nothing whatsoever has deterred from setting their faces toward Him, whom the world has been powerless to hinder, who fulfilled their pledge to His Covenant, and who stood fast in His Cause until their souls took their flight. They bless His loved ones whom the changes and chances of the world have not deterred, whom adversities cannot estrange from His Cause, and who under the blaze of His trials have clung to the cord of patience. They ask that the doubts of the infidels not keep the believer back, that hearts be so strengthened that the power of the unbelievers will not frighten them, and that the friends be endued with such constancy that they arise to proclaim His Cause before all. One confesses that there is no refuge to flee to except God. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá asks that the friends be made like firmly-fixed mountains in the Covenant, unshaken by storms, and presents a servant passionately wandering in the desert of God’s love.

In the catalogue record the paragraph goes on to say that such a one shall be numbered with the inmates of Paradise. The supplied extract differs from the authorized text only in spelling Dayspring as two words, and keeps its approximate status. This supplied extract from Gleanings CXXXIV joins two passages of Bahá’u’lláh. The rest lists the virtues and attributes pertaining unto God that are mentioned in all the heavenly Books, among them forbearance, resignation, contentment, patience and thankfulness in the midst of tribulation, and complete reliance upon Him. Because the two parts come from different contexts, the extract keeps its approximate status. It extends the section on patience.

questions: Bahá’u’lláh calls steadfastness the first word of the Crimson Book and the crown of all deeds, yet also the end of a matter whose beginning is the recognition of God. How do the opening sections help you understand why steadfastness, and not recognition alone, is given such a station?

Bahá’u’lláh defines steadfastness as knowing God alone as the One who prevails over all things, while ‘Abdu’l-Bahá names silence, contentment, deeds and self-sacrifice as its causes and evidence. Which of these seems most within reach in your own circumstances, and why?

‘Abdu’l-Bahá writes that firmness in safety is something even a weak ant can manage, and a reported talk says that without trials nothing is accomplished. Using the sections on mountains, trees and tests, consider how trials reveal steadfastness and how they build it.

The Hidden Words call fortitude under God’s decree the sign of love, and several passages say that in His love every fire is light. How does the section on steadfastness in love change the way the section on patience reads?

‘Abdu’l-Bahá tells the friends that even if he were raised upon the gallows, or news came that the Holy Land had changed, they must grow firmer, and that the condition of steadfastness is following in all things. What do the readings on the Covenant and on faithfulness suggest steadfastness is anchored to?

Several readings say that to enter the Kingdom is easy but to remain is hard, and that many take ten steps and stop. Choose one account from the section on those who stood firm and one counsel on perseverance, and consider what they suggest about steadfastness over the length of a life.
